contributions: Formulates reliability qualification as a partially observable sequential decision problem with per-device latent parameters, and solves it with MCTS over a seed-action simulator coupled to an EKF belief state.
A seed-action abstraction that makes planning over a stochastic simulator exactly reproducible by representing each decision as a pseudorandom seed.

A demonstration that progressive widening decouples tree size from action-grid cardinality: identical 500-node, 30-child trees across a 36-fold range in action count, with yield improving monotonically with grid resolution.
A per-mechanism sensitivity decomposition showing device characterisability is governed by its own BTI parameters, and that additional search budget does not recover an adverse instance.
An objective ablation isolating the safety barrier (catastrophe 46 to 78 percent), early shaping (yield 39 to 31 percent) and the per-epoch cost (25 percent longer tests, no yield change).
limitations: The authors state four: simulation-only validation with a possibly optimistic Gaussian measurement-noise assumption; a single technology calibration point; no model of BTI recovery, which would permit stress-relax protocols; and 38 hours of single-core compute for the full plan, which they defend by the anytime property and by noting rollouts parallelise. They also note the objective constants and mechanism-balance calibration are choices for this study, and that assuming perfect observability of the competing damage states makes the result a performance ceiling for sensor-driven implementations rather than a deployable number. Reader-visible additions: the competing mechanisms are treated through proxy damage indices; the headline yield improvement from 20 to 54 percent is measured across windows of a single converged run, so it conflates planner improvement with the search having already spent budget on that instance; and the perturbation sweeps are single-seed 500-iteration runs whose baseline (14.6 percent) already differs from the main run's first window (20.4 percent) by run-to-run variance comparable to some of the effects being compared.
method: The device is simulated with three concurrent physics-based mechanisms -- bias temperature instability as the characterisation target, electromigration and time-dependent dielectric breakdown as the competing hazards -- each with latent per-device parameters drawn from truncated Normal or log-normal distributions, so every device presents a different degradation landscape. Each decision quantises voltage, current density, temperature and dwell time. To make planning deterministic over a stochastic simulator, an action is represented as a 32-bit pseudorandom seed that deterministically maps to those four values, so replaying a seed sequence from a state reproduces the trajectory exactly. MCTS with UCB1 and progressive widening searches over seed sequences; an extended Kalman filter maintains a belief over the latent parameters from in-test measurements. The reward has a terminal part (20,000 for characterisation success, -2,000 for catastrophe, an uncertainty penalty of 5,000 above target, a timeout penalty scaled by remaining distance) and six shaping terms: progress, early soft shaping, a proximity safety barrier, a damage-increment term, an uncertainty term and a per-epoch living cost. The authors state these constants are calibration choices for this study rather than universal ones.
one_liner: Plans semiconductor reliability stress tests as a partially observable sequential decision problem, using Monte Carlo tree search over a seed-action simulator with an extended Kalman filter tracking per-device latent degradation parameters, so each device's test adapts to its own measured behaviour rather than to a population model.
problem: Qualification testing must push a device hard enough to characterise one degradation mechanism before two competing mechanisms destroy it. Current practice uses static test plans derived from population-level acceleration models, which cannot respond to per-unit variability or to degradation observed during the test, so the plan is either too conservative to characterise or too aggressive and the part fails catastrophically first.

relevance.test-time-scaling: A search-budget study from outside language modelling, and its two structural findings are the ones that transfer. Progressive widening makes the realised search tree independent of the action-space size -- identical node count and branching across a 36-fold range in action cardinality -- so refining the action grid buys resolution without paying combinatorially, which is the opposite of the assumption that a larger space demands proportionally more search. And the budget curve has a condition attached: yield rises smoothly from 15 to 39 percent between 100 and 5,000 iterations on a nominal instance, but on an adverse instance a fourfold budget increase changes nothing, because what binds is the feasibility of the instance rather than the thoroughness of the search. Stated in the archive's terms, more test-time compute pays only where a solution exists within the constraints, and per-instance sensitivity analysis -- not the aggregate scaling curve -- is what tells you which regime you are in. The objective ablation makes a third point that recurs in reasoning work: the shaping terms, not the search, carry most of the safety behaviour, since removing the proximity barrier alone raises the catastrophe rate from 46 to 78 percent.

results: Simulation only. Over 5,000 planning iterations, per-window characterisation yield rises from 20 percent in the first 500-iteration window to 54 percent in the last, with cumulative yield 39.2 percent against 16 percent for a random policy (84 percent catastrophe) and 22 percent for a fixed-stress policy (78 percent). The full outcome split is 39.2 percent success, 55.4 percent catastrophe, 5.4 percent timeout -- so mechanism competition rather than test budget binds, confirmed directly by varying the horizon over 150, 300 and 450 epochs and getting identical results. Belief uncertainty falls from about 0.31 to 0.044 (86 percent), most of it in the first 30 epochs, though this still misses the 0.01 target. The best trajectory runs 119 epochs and shows three self-organised phases -- information gathering below 0.15 damage, damage-aware moderation at 0.3-0.4, then targeted completion that accelerates BTI over the competing mechanisms. Two results transfer beyond the domain. First, budget scaling is smooth and sublinear: 15.0 percent yield at 100 iterations, 20.4 at 500, 25.7 at 1,000, 30.0 at 2,500, 39.2 at 5,000, with about two-thirds of the final yield reached by 1,000 -- and 38 hours of single-core compute for the full run. Second, progressive widening decouples the search from the action space: across coarse, default and fine grids spanning a 36-fold range in action cardinality (24, 288, 875), the realised tree is identical at 500 nodes and 30 root children, because the children expanded at a node are bounded by its visit count rather than by the number of available actions -- so finer resolution raises attainable yield (0.0, 14.6, 29.4 percent) at no combinatorial cost. The perturbation study is the most informative negative result: performance is governed by the device rather than by the planner. A joint +10 percent shift in degradation parameters gives 83.2 percent yield and a -10 percent shift gives 0.0; decomposed per mechanism, BTI alone accounts for nearly all of it (69.6 against 0.0 percent at plus and minus 10 percent) while EM and TDDB move it only modestly. Critically, re-running the adverse case at 1,000 and 2,000 iterations -- a fourfold budget increase -- left the yield unchanged at zero, whereas the nominal device improves with budget. Robustness elsewhere is good: an EKF prior deliberately offset from the true distribution gives 17.0 percent against a 14.6 baseline, and four configurations varying the exploration constant and seed span 34-39 percent. Objective ablation: removing the safety barrier raises catastrophe to 78 percent, removing early shaping drops yield to 31 percent, and removing the per-epoch cost lengthens tests 25 percent without improving yield.
